specPoints.text: know the reactions of: i oxides of Group 1 and 2 elements with water and dilute acid ii hydroxides of Group 1 and 2 elements with dilute acid

primer.text: Metal oxides and hydroxides are bases, and their behaviour with water and dilute acid follows a clean group pattern. This note writes the oxide-water and neutralisation equations for both groups, notes the amphoteric exception at beryllium, and explains why powdered oxide beats a lump when insoluble sulfates crust the surface.

lessons.title: Group 1 oxides and hydroxides with water and acid
sourceHeadings: Reactions of Group 1 oxides with water
Reactions of Group 1 hydroxides with dilute acid
lessons.opening: Group 1 oxides dissolve aggressively, spilling hydroxide ions into water. This lesson writes the oxide-water equation at ionic and formula level, then runs the hydroxides through both standard acids to their salts.
keyPoints: Group 1 oxides react with water giving a colourless alkaline solution.
Sodium oxide adds to water as Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH.
The ionic driver is O2- + H2O -> 2OH-, the same step for both groups.
Hydroxide plus dilute hydrochloric acid gives the chloride: NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O.
Hydroxide plus dilute sulfuric acid gives the sulfate, as in NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + H2O.

low.restatement: Oxide ions grab protons from water, doubling into hydroxide ions; the resulting alkali then swaps partners with any dilute acid to make salt and water.
low.analogy: A sponge (O2-) soaking one proton per side doubles into two smaller sponges (OH-), each then trading its load to an acid for a salt receipt.
low.examPointer: Write the ionic oxide-water step - O2- + H2O -> 2OH- - when asked why the solution is alkaline; the hydroxide release is the answer.

medium.restatement: The oxide's O2- ion is a strong base, abstracting protons quantitatively from water; the neutralisation that follows with HCl or H2SO4 is stoichiometric, so one NaOH handles one HCl while two NaOH handle one H2SO4.
medium.analogy: A two-seater sofa (H2SO4) needs two guests (two NaOH) to seat fully, while the single chair (HCl) needs one - stoichiometry is seating capacity.
medium.examPointer: Balance the sulfate products: 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O - two waters, not one, when the acid carries two protons.

check.stem: What solution results when sodium oxide reacts with water?

options.text: A colourless alkaline solution of sodium hydroxide
options.explanation: The released OH- makes it alkaline.
The oxide is basic, not acidic.

options.text: A white precipitate of sodium oxide

check.stem: Which ionic equation captures the oxide-in-water step?

options.explanation: The oxide ion protonates once and splits into two hydroxides.
That is neutralisation, not the water reaction.

check.stem: What are the products when sodium hydroxide meets dilute sulfuric acid?

options.explanation: The sulfate salt plus the neutralisation water.
Hydrogen needs a metal above it in the series, not an acid-base pair.
Sulfite implies SO3 2-, not the sulfate.

check.stem: Why is the NaOH + HCl equation a neutralisation?

options.text: The alkali's hydroxide meets the acid's hydrogen ion to form water and a salt
options.explanation: That pairing is the neutralisation definition.
Acid-base chemistry transfers protons, not electrons.

check.stem: How many moles of NaOH neutralise one mole of H2SO4?

options.explanation: The diprotic acid needs two hydroxides.
One hydroxide seats only one proton.

check.stem: Write the equation for sodium oxide with water.
check.modelAnswer: Na2O (s) + H2O (l) -> 2NaOH (aq), a colourless alkaline solution.

check.stem: State the ionic step that releases hydroxide ions in water.
check.modelAnswer: O2- + H2O -> 2OH-, the step shared by Group 1 and Group 2 oxides.

check.stem: Explain why the oxide solution is alkaline.
check.modelAnswer: The oxide ion abstracts protons from water, releasing free hydroxide ions; any solution carrying excess OH- is alkaline by definition.

check.stem: Neutralising 0.5 moles of H2SO4 needs how many moles of NaOH, and how many moles of water form?
check.modelAnswer: Two hydroxides per acid give 1.0 mole of NaOH and 1.0 mole of water from the doubled stoichiometry.

lessons.title: Group 2 oxides: water, acid and the amphoteric outlier
sourceHeadings: Reactions of Group 2 oxides with water
lessons.opening: Group 2 oxides are bases - beryllium's the exception that leans both ways. This lesson reads the oxide-water table's pH climb, then shows why insoluble sulfates crust the surface and how powder plus stirring keeps the reaction alive.
keyPoints: All Group 2 oxides are basic except BeO, which is amphoteric.
Oxides react with water forming alkaline solutions that grow more alkaline down the group.
MgO dissolves only slightly, giving a weakly alkaline solution around pH 10.
CaO reacts vigorously and exothermically, its lump seeming to expand and open.
Insoluble sulfates form on the oxide surface with sulfuric acid; powdering and stirring limit the crust.

low.restatement: Down the group the oxides dissolve more readily, so their solutions carry more hydroxide and climb in pH; with sulfuric acid, the insoluble sulfate product can seal the oxide before the reaction finishes.
low.analogy: A wick that soaks better as it thickens (solubility climb), dipped in wax that hardens around it (sulfate crust) - powdering keeps the wick exposed.
low.examPointer: Name the amphoteric exception - BeO - explicitly in any 'all Group 2 oxides are basic' statement.

medium.restatement: Hydroxide solubility rises down the group, raising OH- concentration and pH from MgO's weak 10 to BaO's strong alkaline solution; the sulfate crust is a kinetics problem - the product layer blocks acid contact, which fine powder and stirring mitigate by refreshing the surface.
medium.analogy: A moat forming around a castle: the sulfate ring cuts the acid off from the oxide keep; grinding the stone into gravel keeps the moat from closing.
medium.examPointer: Quote pH 10 for magnesium oxide's solution and 'vigorous, exothermic' for calcium oxide when reading the table in answers.

check.stem: Which Group 2 oxide is amphoteric rather than basic?

options.explanation: Beryllium oxide acts as acid and base alike.

check.stem: How does the alkalinity of oxide-water solutions trend down Group 2?

options.explanation: Higher hydroxide solubility drives the climb.

options.text: It depends on the acid present
options.explanation: No acid participates in the water reaction.

check.stem: What observation accompanies calcium oxide reacting with water?

options.text: A vigorous, exothermic reaction that boils some water as the lump expands
options.explanation: The table's observation line in action.
No gas forms in the water reaction.

check.stem: Why does the reaction of a Group 2 oxide with sulfuric acid slow down and stop?

options.text: Insoluble sulfate forms on the oxide surface, blocking acid contact
options.explanation: The product layer cuts the reactants apart.

options.text: The water product dissolves the acid
options.explanation: Water dilutes but never stops it.

check.stem: Which practical measures limit the sulfate crust problem?

options.text: Powdering the oxide and stirring the mixture

options.explanation: Concentration does not breach the crust.

check.stem: Write the equation for calcium oxide with water.
check.modelAnswer: CaO (s) + H2O (l) -> Ca(OH)2 (s), a vigorous reaction releasing much energy.

check.stem: State the solubility and pH of magnesium oxide's water solution.
check.modelAnswer: MgO is only slightly soluble, forming a weakly alkaline solution around pH 10.

check.stem: Explain why the oxide-water solutions grow more alkaline down the group.
check.modelAnswer: Hydroxide solubility rises down the group, so each oxide's water solution carries more dissolved OH- and reads a higher pH.

check.stem: If MgO's solution sits at pH 10 and BaO's at pH 13, how many times more hydroxide concentration does the barium solution carry?
check.modelAnswer: Three pH units mean 10 to the power 3, so the barium solution carries about 1000 times the hydroxide concentration.

lessons.title: Group 2 hydroxides against the dilute acids
sourceHeadings: Reactions of Group 2 hydroxides with dilute acid
Group 2 Hydroxide Reactions with Dilute Acids
lessons.opening: Each Group 2 hydroxide neutralises HCl to a chloride and H2SO4 to a sulfate - and the sulfate solubility decides which products stay dissolved. This lesson reads the acid table and flags the insoluble endmembers.
keyPoints: Group 2 hydroxides form colourless solutions of metal salts with dilute acids.
With HCl the products are the chloride and water: Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + 2H2O.
With H2SO4 the products are the sulfate and water: Mg(OH)2 + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + 2H2O.
Sulfate solubility falls down the group, so SrSO4 and BaSO4 appear as solids.
Barium sulfate is the classic insoluble white precipitate of the group.

low.restatement: Hydroxide plus acid always yields salt plus water; whether the salt stays dissolved is the sulfate trend's business - soluble at the top, precipitating white at the bottom.
low.analogy: Two checkout lanes: hydrochloric always clears its items (soluble chlorides), sulfuric jams at the last two lanes (insoluble Sr and Ba sulfates).
low.examPointer: Write state symbols in sulfate answers - (aq) for Mg/Ca, (s) for Sr/Ba - the states carry the trend information.

medium.restatement: The neutralisation stoichiometry doubles for HCl (two protons absorbed per hydroxide pair) while H2SO4 pairs one-to-one; the sulfate trend overlays solubility on top, turning the bottom of the table into precipitate chemistry.
medium.analogy: Two vending machines restocking the same shelf: the chloride machine never jams, the sulfate machine jams progressively from strontium downward.
medium.examPointer: Answer 'insoluble white precipitate of barium sulfate' in full - colour, identity and state all earn marks.

check.stem: What colour are the salt solutions from Group 2 hydroxides and dilute acids?

options.explanation: The salt solutions are colourless throughout.
Blue belongs to copper salts, not Group 2.
Solutions are colourless; the solids are white.

check.stem: What are the products of Ca(OH)2 with dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.explanation: The chloride salt plus neutralisation water.
That is the sulfuric acid route.

check.stem: Which two sulfates appear as solids in the acid table?
Why does the sulfate solubility trend matter in these reactions?

options.text: Falling sulfate solubility turns the lower group's products into white precipitates

options.explanation: Stoichiometry is fixed by the acid's protons.

options.text: It affects the chloride products too

check.stem: What is the observation when Ba(OH)2 meets dilute sulfuric acid?

options.text: A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms
options.explanation: The insoluble salt appears as the reaction runs.

check.stem: Write the equation for Mg(OH)2 with dilute sulfuric acid.
Describe barium sulfate's appearance and solubility.
check.modelAnswer: Barium sulfate is an insoluble white precipitate, the least soluble sulfate of the group.

check.stem: Explain why one hydroxide formula unit absorbs two HCl molecules but only one H2SO4 molecule.
check.modelAnswer: Each HCl donates one proton, so a two-hydroxide formula unit needs two; H2SO4 carries both protons internally, so one molecule seats the pair.

check.stem: Neutralising 0.1 moles of Ba(OH)2 with HCl needs how many moles of acid, and how many moles of water result?
check.modelAnswer: Two HCl per hydroxide gives 0.2 moles of acid and 0.2 moles of water.

glossary.definition: Describing BeO, which can act as both an acid and a base, unlike the other Group 2 oxides.
Calcium hydroxide solution, the classic alkaline test reagent for carbon dioxide.
The insoluble sulfate layer that forms on an oxide surface in sulfuric acid and blocks further reaction.
